health_cms_sidebar.item_crm_dashboard
Six clickable KPI cards plus a contact-status donut, a source-channel bar chart and three live feeds, all filtered by one period selector.
It is the only screen that tells you whether the desk is keeping up. Pending Follow-ups above your team's capacity is the earliest visible sign that somebody will be forgotten.
At the start of every shift, and again before you leave. Not while you are working a single person — use Care Command or Contacts for that.
You need the Owner or CRM role; this leaf is role-gated in the database.
Reading a percentage without the period. Conversion Rate is a month figure; Contacts Today is a day figure. They never describe the same window.
Treating a low Spam Rate as good news. A low rate can also mean nobody is marking spam, which quietly inflates every other number.
Not clicking through. Every card and every chart segment opens the exact records behind it — a surprising number should always be opened, never explained away.

health_care_command.item_care_command
One work item per person, merged from Zalo, calls, email and web chat, ordered by a computed urgency score.
Without it, four inboxes each look quiet while the same family is waiting in all four. The wall is the only place the whole picture exists.
All shift. It is where a CRM operator lives; the other screens are what you open from it.
Owner or CRM role, plus at least one connected channel. Taking a conversation off a colleague additionally needs CRM Manager.
Replying without claiming. Two operators answering the same family within a minute of each other is the most common complaint this screen exists to prevent.
Reading the urgency score as a clinical severity. It is a triage number built from status and waiting time. A 110 is not a medical emergency; it is a strong queue position.
Assuming the Zalo account belongs to the patient. In home care it is very often a son or a daughter — and what you may tell them is a consent question, not a convenience question.

phone
outline
health_cms_sidebar.item_crm_contacts
carecommand
Every enquiry as a record, filtered by lifecycle status, with Book · Log Activity · Log as Lead · Escalate · Spam · Booking Lost on each row and on the form.
Care Command is the queue; this is the ledger. A conversation can be closed, but the contact's status is what the Dashboard counts and what the next operator inherits.
When you need the whole person rather than the current message — booking them in, recording why a booking was lost, or checking what a colleague did last week.
Owner or CRM role. Booking additionally needs a service, a facility and a date/time.
Skipping the duplicate check in the booking wizard. Confirming the wrong suggested client writes the visit — and later the clinical note — into another person's record.
Using Spam as a way to clear the list. Spam also flags the phone number, so a real family member is pre-judged the next time they call.
Leaving a lost booking un-reasoned. “Booking Lost” without a reason is invisible to Lead Analysis, so the same cause repeats all quarter.

health_cms_sidebar.item_crm_activities
contacts
Everything anyone scheduled on a contact, grouped by type (To-Do · Email · Call · Meeting · Document) with a type filter and a date filter.
A promise made on Monday is only kept if it is visible on Thursday. This board is the difference between “we'll call you back” and being called back.
Twice a day: at the start of the shift, and before handover at {{handoverTime}}. Also whenever the Dashboard's Pending Follow-ups number surprises you.
Owner or CRM role. An activity must be scheduled on a contact — it cannot exist on its own.
Scheduling on yourself out of habit. An activity assigned to one person is invisible as team work; if you are off sick it simply does not happen.
Closing an activity without recording the outcome on the contact. The board goes green, the contact's status stays wrong, and the Dashboard lies.
Filtering to Today and forgetting overdue items are not in that filter.

An immutable record of exactly what arrived — a Facebook comment with no phone, a webhook with no identity. You convert it or dismiss it; you cannot edit it.
A queue nobody can find is a queue that does not exist. These are real people who reached out and would otherwise vanish between systems.
Once or twice a shift, and always after a campaign goes live — that is when the volume of half-identified arrivals jumps.
Visible to every role. Converting needs at least one anchor: a contact, a phone number or an email address.
Dismissing to clear the badge. Dismissal is an answer — “this was not a patient” — and it is recorded against your name.
Trying to correct what arrived. The record is deliberately un-editable: it is evidence of what the channel actually sent.
Converting a capture with no anchor and being surprised it refuses — there would be no way to reach the person again.

health_care_command_channels.item_channel_center
A catalogue of the eight connectable channels with a lifecycle state each, the readiness checks behind that state, and the go-live console.
Configured is not connected. A channel that leaves the connected states stops sending and can stop receiving — and nothing queues. Patients get silence, and the wall looks calm.
At go-live, when a grant is expiring, and the moment a channel's traffic drops to zero. Not during a shift by a shift operator.
Visible to every role, but the state has exactly one writer — a server transition path. You cannot type a state in.
Choosing the wrong Official Account at the “choose what to connect” step. One OA serves one catchment area, so the wrong one routes a whole city's messages into another city's wall.
Ignoring “Expiring soon”. It still sends today, which is exactly why it gets ignored until the day it does not.
Reading a green tick as proof of delivery. The readiness checks prove the connection is capable; only real traffic proves it works.

One row per website arrival: page, referrer, UTM source/medium/campaign, and the Google or Facebook click id — plus an “Unmatched campaigns” chip for arrivals with no tags.
It is the only honest answer to “which advert is actually producing bookings”. Without it, budget follows opinion.
Weekly, and whenever a campaign's cost per enquiry looks wrong. Also when a specific person asks “how did you get my number”.
Visible to every role. A touchpoint is created by the website connector; you never type one in.
Assuming the touchpoint and the conversation share a channel. Someone can click a Google advert on Monday and message Zalo on Wednesday; they are joined by phone number, not by channel.
Treating “Unmatched campaigns” as noise. It is usually a link somebody published without tags — a fixable, repeating leak.
Counting touchpoints as people. One person browsing four pages is four touchpoints and one enquiry.

The Dashboard tells you the number. This tells you which combination produced it — which channel, in which area, for which service.
Monthly review, campaign post-mortems, and any argument about where enquiries come from.
Visible to every role. Numbers only reconcile with the Dashboard if you match the period and the catchment filter.
Comparing this month's pivot with the Dashboard's Today card and calling it a discrepancy.
Grouping by declared channel when the traffic says otherwise. Effective channel is the field that reflects what actually happened.
Reading a small cell as a trend. Six referrals in a month is a number, not a pattern.
